summary:
Bermuda is a British Overseas Territory whose domestic legislation governs. The United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and its single-sex services provisions do not extend to Bermuda automatically and could be applied only by Order in Council, so the operative framework for a trans visitor is Bermudian law rather than United Kingdom equality law.

There is no legal recognition of transgender people in Bermuda. The Human Rights Act has prohibited discrimination on the ground of sexual orientation since 2013, when the Senate passed the Human Rights Amendment Act (which also banned age discrimination), after proposals in 2004 to 2006 and in 2009 failed or were dropped. Gender identity is not a protected ground, so no statutory protection against discrimination on the basis of gender identity exists.

Sources record no transgender-specific provisions on identity documents, screening, facilities, custody, healthcare, enforcement, penalties or protection machinery. The single documented instance of official restriction on gender expression is the Government's 2006 attempt to bar Mark Anderson, the drag performer known as Sybil, from taking part in a parade on the ground that the performer contradicted local mores and sensitivities. Expression of gender identity is described as often difficult.

Marriage equality was revoked. The Supreme Court legalised same-sex marriage in May 2017 in the Godwin and DeRoche marriage-licence case under the Marriage Act 1944 and the Human Rights Act. The Domestic Partnership Act 2017, given assent on 7 February 2018 and effective 1 June 2018, replaced marriage with domestic partnerships for both same-sex and heterosexual couples, the first time a jurisdiction revoked marriage equality. The Supreme Court restored marriage on 6 June 2018 and the Court of Appeal on 23 November 2018, and the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council upheld the ban on 14 March 2022, with legislation of July 2022 operating retrospectively over the intervening period. Same-sex marriage has not been available since 2022; domestic partnerships are. A trans visitor in a relationship that Bermudian law would class as same-sex cannot marry in Bermuda and would be limited to a domestic partnership.

Consensual sex between adult men was decriminalised in 1994 by the Stubbs Bill, carried in the House of Assembly by 22 votes to 16. Anal and oral sex had previously carried liability of up to ten years' imprisonment. Sexual activity between women has never been illegal.

State posture toward sexual-orientation offences has been active. In November 2020 reporting, the Government had spent approximately £150,000 appealing a case in which a man was charged and threatened with jail under the "obscene behaviour law" for importing DVDs of gay pornography, a case that had been found unconstitutional.
tangentialFactors:
Organised religious opposition to visible same-sex couples is documented. The African Methodist Episcopal church and other churches protested the arrival of the gay cruise ship Norwegian Dawn on a New York to Bermuda sailing in July 2005, describing it as incompatible with "the word of God and the Christian moral fibre". The 1994 decriminalisation debate split the island, with religious leaders divided and the Christian Coalition staging marches against the change.

Both episodes concern visitors and residents who are visibly read as same-sex couples rather than trans travellers specifically; no comparable organised campaign directed at transgender people appears in the inventory.
localsOnly:
The age of consent is unequal. It stands at 18 for consensual anal intercourse under the law effective 1 November 2019, against 16 for other sexual activity. The earlier higher age of 18 for gay male conduct was found to violate the European Convention on Human Rights, and the Criminal Code provision on gross indecency between men was repealed in 2019.

Same-sex couples may adopt on the same terms as others under the Adoption of Children Act, following a February 2015 Supreme Court ruling on marital-status and sexual-orientation discrimination. Binational same-sex partners were granted equal employment and benefits by the Supreme Court in November 2015.

The Bermuda Regiment is raised by random lottery-style conscription. It does not discriminate on grounds of sexual orientation and officially prohibits discrimination or harassment of LGBT soldiers. Reported practice has been otherwise: such conduct has been described as tolerated by officers, and one conscript described the Regiment as "the most homophobic environment that exists".

Gay and bisexual men may donate blood with the Bermuda Hospitals Board if they have not had sex with another man in the previous 12 months. The same 12-month deferral applies to women who have sexual relations with men who have sex with men.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory records an absence of transgender-specific provisions rather than a documented policy. It contains no material on how identity documents or gender markers are issued or changed, on immigration and entry screening, on airport or border screening practice, on facilities and custody, or on healthcare access. An absence of recorded provisions is not evidence that no practice exists in any of these areas.

The July 2022 legislation operated retrospectively over the period in which marriage equality had been in force. What that means for couples who married during that window is not stated in the inventory and is unresolved.

The inventory does not state whether the Human Rights Act's omission of gender identity has been the subject of litigation, a proposed amendment, or a complaints decision. Unresolved.

No trans-specific violence data for Bermuda appears in the inventory, and no incident-level reporting specific to transgender residents or visitors is present.
